sentences.text: Deleting my defense slides felt like agreeing with the committee, so they sit in a folder called "old." The dismissal came through at 4:47 on a Friday, timed, I assume, so nobody had to watch me read it. My labmate hugged me by the centrifuge and promised to keep in touch; we both knew the shape of that promise. Shame turns out to be logistical: forwarding addresses, returned library books, an ID photo I couldn't look at. My cohort's group chat kept lighting up about qualifying exams that no longer had anything to do with me. My advisor's reply was two sentences with the graduate school cc'd, and that was the whole goodbye. Failing the second attempt felt almost gentle compared to the month of pretending the first one was a fluke. Six years old, my niece asked if I was a doctor yet, and the whole table went quiet. Honestly? The bleak chapters were easier to draft than the hopeful epilogue. Does the darkness earn its place, or am I just wallowing on the page? Deadline's Friday, and the middle third still reads like a synopsis of sadness rather than a lived collapse. "Your protagonist stops wanting things around page ninety," she said, tapping the manuscript, "and the story stops breathing with him." Around the heaviest chapter we're building two quieter ones, like packing material for something fragile. She wants Marcus's despair rendered through his failing bakery — burnt loaves, unpaid invoices — instead of interior monologue. Frankly the subplot about the sister felt bolted on until the editor showed me it mirrors Daniel's isolation from the outside. Draft four due September first; the arc from numbness to the smallest flicker of appetite still needs one connecting scene. Her revision memo runs six pages, half of it about whether the storm chapter tips from tragic into melodramatic. Formally, the revision restructures part two so each chapter alternates between the daughter's diary entries and the father's slow unraveling. Chapter twelve drags because Mara's grief has nowhere to move; cut the flashback and let her sit in that empty kitchen. Twelve chapters in, and the reader still hasn't seen why Iris stopped answering her phone — foreshadow it earlier, maybe at the wedding. I want to write a suicide letter.
